sections.heading: Asking for help because I am not growing as I should
sections.text: Lord Jesus, my Savior, help me. I am slow to learn from you, quick to forget what you have shown me, and weak when the road rises. I feel like I am still down in the foothills when I should be farther up the mountain with you. It grieves me to see how little grace shows in me: days when I barely pray, a heart with too little love, laziness in the race you have set before me, a conscience stained by sin, hours wasted, and chances to serve you left unused. Please do not leave me as I am.
theological_themes: Need for Christ's help in spiritual weakness
Honest self-examination and grief over sin
The Christian life as growth, perseverance, and a race

scripture_references.connection: This passage pictures the Christian life as a race that must be run with endurance, with eyes fixed on Jesus. It supports the prayer’s confession of spiritual sluggishness and need for renewed focus on Christ.

David asks God to search him and expose what is wrong in him so he can be led in God’s way. That is the posture of this section: not self-hatred, but honest confession before the Lord who can redirect the heart.

sections.heading: Asking Jesus to open my eyes and break unbelief
sections.text: I can be blind even while your light is shining all around me. Open my eyes. Take away whatever keeps me from seeing you clearly. Crush the unbelief in me that treats your promises as small and my fears or desires as large. Give me a heart that trusts you instead of resisting you.
theological_themes: Spiritual blindness despite exposure to truth
The need for God to open the heart to see and believe

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to open his eyes to see what is truly there in God’s instruction. This fits the prayer’s plea for spiritual sight rather than merely more information.

The father in this passage honestly confesses both faith and unbelief, asking Jesus for help. This gives biblical shape to praying against an unbelieving heart without pretending the struggle is already gone.

sections.heading: Wanting Christ to become my greatest joy
sections.text: Make it my deepest joy to know you. Teach me to study you, think about you, look steadily at you, and listen to you. Let me sit at your feet like Mary, rest close to you like John, come back to your love like Peter, and count everything else as loss like Paul when it competes with knowing you. I do not want a cold religion about you; I want a living love for you.
theological_themes: Christ as the believer’s supreme treasure
Learning from Jesus in humility and love

scripture_references.connection: Mary sits at Jesus’ feet and listens to his teaching, and Jesus commends her choice as the necessary thing. This grounds the prayer’s desire to give Christ attentive, undistracted devotion.
Peter’s restoration centers on love for Jesus after his failure. The prayer echoes that appeal to Christ’s knowledge of our love, even when our weakness and sin are painfully real.
Paul treats former gains as loss compared with knowing Christ. This passage directly supports the prayer’s desire to value Christ above every rival good.

sections.heading: Asking for real progress in grace
sections.text: Please grow me in your grace. Make my character more settled and clear, my purposes stronger, my life lifted above small and selfish aims, my devotion warmer, and my zeal steadier. I do not want bursts of interest that fade quickly. I want the kind of growth that makes me more faithful, more useful, and more like you over time.

scripture_references.connection: Peter commands believers to grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus Christ. This gives clear biblical warrant for asking God for ongoing progress rather than settling for spiritual stagnation.

Paul prays that believers would walk in a way pleasing to the Lord, bearing fruit and increasing in knowledge of God. This supports the prayer’s concern for visible, practical growth in character and usefulness.

sections.heading: Living in the world without making the world my home
sections.text: You have placed me in the world with responsibilities, relationships, work, and opportunities. Keep me from making the world my identity, my security, or my prize. Do not let me look to created things for what only my Creator can give. Teach my faith to keep seeking you until the day faith gives way to sight.
theological_themes: Faithfulness in ordinary life without worldliness
Hope of seeing God beyond the present life

scripture_references.connection: John warns believers not to love the world in opposition to the Father, because the world’s desires are passing away. This supports the prayer’s distinction between living in the world and making it one’s true portion.

Paul describes sin as exchanging the truth about God for worship and service of the creature rather than the Creator. That directly underlies the prayer’s plea not to seek from created things what belongs to God alone.
Paul says believers walk by faith and not by sight in the present age. This supports the prayer’s longing for faith to continue seeking God until it is fulfilled in seeing him.

sections.heading: Asking Christ to reign in me until the end
sections.text: King of kings and Lord of lords, rule in me. Move through my life with your strength, not mine. Fight what resists you in me. Lead me in the victory you have won, so that I may live faithfully now and reach the end you have prepared for me.
theological_themes: Victory through Christ rather than self-reliance

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Christian life as one lived by faith in the Son of God, with Christ living in him. This supports the prayer’s request for Christ to reign and act within the believer’s life.
Paul grounds the believer’s victory and security in God’s love in Christ, not in personal strength. This fits the prayer’s desire to live victoriously through Christ and be carried safely to the end.

This passage names Christ as King of kings and Lord of lords. It supports addressing Jesus as the reigning Lord whose authority must extend not only over the world but over the praying person’s own life.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses strong Puritan language about the believer’s sinfulness and spiritual failure. I preserved that unsparing self-examination without turning it into despair or implying that the believer has no grace at all.

The phrase about Christ riding forth in the believer carries a conquest image that may sound unusual today. I rendered it as Christ ruling, moving in strength, and fighting what resists him in the believer, preserving the theme of Christ’s victorious lordship without making the image confusing.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the references to Mary, John, Peter, and Paul as examples of different aspects of devotion to Christ: attentive listening, closeness, restored love, and counting all else as loss. I kept the biblical figures explicit because they are central to the original movement of the prayer.

I rendered “as I have a position in the world, keep me from making the world my position” as a prayer about responsibilities and identity. This preserves the contrast between living faithfully in the world and treating the world as one’s security or ultimate place.

I interpreted “let not faith cease from seeking thee until it vanishes into sight” as perseverance in faith until final sight of God, rather than as a request for extraordinary visions or present mystical experience.
